title: Making plans to meet
goal: Invite, accept and turn down invitations; agree on a time and place; talk about the weather.
bekal: agreeing on a time and meeting place

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Quedamos el sábado
dialogs.intro: Making a date: inviting, negotiating the time, agreeing on a place.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Oye, ¿te apetece ir al cine el sábado?
lines.id: Hey, do you fancy going to the cinema on Saturday?
lines.literal: listen, to-you appeals go to-the cinema the Saturday?

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.id: OK! What time shall we meet?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: La película empieza a las ocho. ¿Quedamos a las siete y media?
lines.id: The film starts at eight. Shall we meet at half past seven?
lines.literal: the film it-begins at the eight. we-arrange at the seven and half?

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Uf, a las siete y media no puedo. Trabajo hasta las siete.
lines.id: Ugh, I can't do half past seven. I work until seven.
lines.literal: ugh, at the seven and half not I-can. I-work until the seven.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Entonces a las ocho menos cuarto, en la puerta del cine.
lines.id: Then at a quarter to eight, at the cinema door.
lines.literal: then at the eight minus quarter, at the door of-the cinema.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.id: Perfect. And afterwards shall we have dinner?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Me encantaría. Conozco un sitio muy bueno.
lines.id: I'd love to. I know a really good place.
lines.literal: to-me would-please-much. I-know a place very good.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.id: Is it far? I don't have a car.
lines.literal: it-is-located far? because not I-have car.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: No, está al lado. Diez minutos andando.
lines.id: No, it's close. Ten minutes on foot.
lines.literal: no, it-is-located at-the side. ten minutes walking.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Genial. ¿Qué tiempo va a hacer el sábado?
lines.id: Great. What's the weather going to be like on Saturday?
lines.literal: great. what weather it-goes to make the Saturday?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Va a hacer bueno. Sol y veinticinco grados.
lines.id: It's going to be nice. Sunny and twenty-five degrees.
lines.literal: it-goes to make good. sun and twenty-five degrees.

notes: **Oye** = "hey", "listen", a very common conversation opener among friends. The polite form is *oiga*, used more to call a waiter or a stranger.

**¿Te apetece…?** = "do you feel like…?" — the gentlest and most common way to invite someone in Spain. The pattern is exactly like *gustar*: *me apetece*, *te apetece*, *le apetece*. In Latin America *¿tienes ganas de…?* is more usual.

**Quedar = to arrange to meet.** *¿Quedamos a las siete?* — shall we meet at seven? *Hemos quedado* — we've arranged to meet. It's the most important social verb in everyday Spanish, and it has no one-word English equivalent.

**Saying no without saying no.** Spaniards rarely give a bare *no*. The formula: a short groan (*uf*, *qué pena*) + a reason + a counteroffer. *A las siete y media no puedo, trabajo hasta las siete. ¿A las ocho?*
**Me encantaría** = "I'd love to" — a conditional form, B1 grammar. Learn it whole; it's the warmest answer to an invitation.

**Conocer vs saber.** Both mean "to know". *Conocer* is for people and places you're **familiar with** (*conozco un sitio*, *conozco a Marta*); *saber* is for facts and skills (*sé dónde está*, *sé nadar*). Their *yo* forms are naughty: *conozco*, *sé*.
**Andando** = walking, on foot. This -ando / -iendo form matches English "-ing", and you'll meet it again in *estoy comiendo* (I'm eating). For now, just recognize it in *diez minutos andando*.
**Temperatures use grados.** *Veinticinco grados*, *tres grados bajo cero* (three below zero). Always Celsius.

grammars.title: The weather — el tiempo
body: Weather is described with three verbs that have no subject at all. Which one is used is a matter of habit, not rules, so learn them in groups:
after: Asking: *¿Qué tiempo hace?* (now) or *¿Qué tiempo va a hacer mañana?* (tomorrow). Note that *tiempo* here means weather, not time.
*Llover* and *nevar* also split in the middle, like the verbs in Unit 14: *llueve* from *llover*, *nieva* from *nevar*. But since rain has no subject, these are the only forms you'll ever need.

head: Inviting
Meaning
rows: Do you want to come with me?
¿Qué tal si vamos a la playa?
How about going to the beach?

head: Accepting
Declining
rows: Uf, ese día no me viene bien.

blocks.text: Notice that the right-hand column almost never stops at no: nearly every reply offers another day. Declining without offering an alternative sounds like shutting the door.

blocks.title: Weekends that start on Friday night
items: Spanish evenings start late and end late. Meeting friends for dinner at 10 p.m. is normal, and bars only fill up after midnight.

*El puente* — "the bridge" — is when a public holiday falls on a Tuesday or Thursday, so the working day in between is taken off too. When two holidays are close together, people call it an *acueducto*.
Every town has its own yearly *fiestas*, sometimes a whole week long, and nearly all of them are linked to the town's patron saint. During that week, don't expect offices to keep normal hours.
Invitations in Spain are often last-minute — a message on Saturday morning for Saturday evening is normal, not rude. On the other hand, plans made three weeks ahead often need confirming again.
